claims.text: The starting material is additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy.
The starting alloy has an fcc matrix.
Elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases promotes nanoscale deformation-twin formation in this alloy.
Elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases causes dislocation migration in this alloy.
Nanoscale deformation twins govern degradation of the exposed alloy.
Dislocation migration governs degradation of the exposed alloy.
Formation or growth of deformation twins is associated with accumulating internal elastic stresses.
Dislocation migration leads to accumulation of internal stresses.
Twin formation and dislocation migration create high-energy sites.
Accumulated internal stresses and high-energy sites can cause catastrophic failure.
Exposure between 500 and 1000 °C in air or hydrogen is an applicable range for the proposed twin- and dislocation-mediated behavior.
Elevated-temperature environmental exposure will degrade the alloy relative to its unexposed, as-fabricated baseline.
The degradation may culminate in catastrophic failure.
The baseline is the as-fabricated alloy without elevated-temperature or reactive-gas exposure.
Comparing inert, oxidizing, and reducing exposures while measuring microhardness, diffraction, and TEM features is the proposed controlled test.
Failure to observe degradation or catastrophic failure under the specified conditions would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: Catastrophic failure is presented only as a potential outcome and its required temperature and gas conditions are explicitly uncertain, yet absence of catastrophic failure under the broadly specified test conditions is treated as falsifying.

The hypothesis identifies twins and dislocation migration as the governing mediators, but the falsification rule tests only degradation or failure and does not require measurement or absence of those proposed mediators.
